label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
Here's a draft. I've kept it in your voice — plain, dry, a bit wry — and leaned on the toast and the stairwell rather than on the emotions, so it should read as reflective rather than maudlin. It's about 1,500 words.

---

# The 4am Toast

Last Saturday I worked my last ever night shift. 21:00 to 07:30, majors, the usual run. I clocked off at half past seven, walked out into the car park, and sat in the car with the engine off for longer than I needed to.

The sun was coming up over the London Road. There was a shipping forecast on Radio 4 — on catch-up from the night before, something about dogfish and easterly winds — and I listened to the whole thing, start to finish, like it was important.

And then it occurred to me, quite calmly, that I would not see that light again from this side.

Same sun, obviously. I wasn't going to lose the sun. But I have spent fourteen years on the other side of it, and from Monday I will be on the other side of it along with everybody else, and there is no putting it back.

That is the bit I keep trying to write about and failing at. So let me start again, more slowly.

---

The first one was in 2012. I was an SHO, I was twenty-eight, and I had no idea what I had walked into. I remember thinking: this is a bit strange, everyone looks half-asleep, why does nobody talk at normal volume. I remember the handover being faster than I could follow and me thinking I'd catch up by Wednesday.

I did not catch up by Wednesday. You don't catch up. You just get slower and more careful, which turns out to be the same thing.

Fourteen years. Seven hundred-odd nights, give or take a few I took off for weddings and a hungover Sunday. People ask, when they ask at all, whether I don't get tired. The honest answer is that I got very tired, and then very good at tired, which is a different skill and not one I recommend. You can train it out of yourself. I trained it into myself and then my knees and my blood pressure filed a complaint with my GP, and that complaint was upheld.

---

Our charge nurse on nights is Folasade. Twenty-two years of nights. She still beats me up the stairs and I am forty-two and she is not, and she has never once let me forget the time we heard her shouting "hull" in the resuscitation bay for a patient who was, to be fair, genuinely about to go off. She will still be there on Monday. I will be on days. The rotas will not be the same shape and she will not be on my team any more, and I do not know quite what to do with that.

The thing nobody tells you about a night shift is how much of it is not medicine.

---

Here is what nights gave me.

Nights are where the department is most itself. Fewer managers, fewer daytime politics, fewer people around with an opinion about who said what to whom. On nights the consultants are in the corridor. The porters know your coffee order. The staff from the other departments stop pretending they don't like us and start pretending they don't, which is a great improvement. There is a kind of honesty available at 3am that simply is not available at 11am, and I have never worked out exactly why, but I think it's because everyone is too tired to perform.

My regulars know this, I think. The ones who read this. You have all met me at 3am and you have all met me at 10am and I promise you we are not the same person.

And there is kindness at night that is a different species from daytime kindness, because it costs more. Daytime kindness has energy behind it. Night kindness is what you have left when you are empty. The night staff are the ones who hold the hand and bring the tea and say the small thing that stops someone's whole night from being unbearable, and they do it on no sleep, and almost nobody sees it happen.

People think nights are about adrenaline. Occasionally, once a year, maybe. Mostly it is about staying kind at 5am when you have nothing left.

---

Here is what nights took.

The first winter, I cried in the car park at the Infirmary. Not for any reason I could have explained to a colleague — nobody had been unkind, nothing had gone badly. I was sitting in the car because I could not remember whether I had given the second dose. I had. I checked. I had given it, it was in the notes, it was fine.

I still remember the frost on the windscreen. I remember thinking: if I had not given it, what would I have done. And then I remember thinking: I do not even remember giving it, so what else have I not remembered. Nights do that to you. They take away the memory of the thing you most need to remember, and then they give it back, hours later, in the shower, at 4pm, with the specific relief of someone who has just been reprieved.

I missed both of my nieces' naming ceremonies, over video, in Bangalore, because I was on nights. My sister has never once complained about it. She has never even mentioned it. She is a better person than I am and I have never worked out how she manages it, and I have not asked, because I am fairly sure I would not enjoy the answer.

---

And then last winter, at about 3am, an old gentleman held my hand and told me I had his daughter's hands.

I will not tell you anything else about him, because he is not mine to tell, and because there is nothing in his story that anyone needs except the fact that it happened and that he was kind to me when I was tired and slightly useless. He went home three days later. That is the whole of it. I have thought about it more than I have thought about most of the medicine I have ever done.

---

Here is the thing I cannot make fit into a sentence properly.

I am relieved. My knees are grateful. My blood pressure is, in the words of a man I respect, no longer a joke. I sleep on Sunday nights now. I will see the sun coming up over the London Road from the correct side of the clock, on the way *to* work, like a person.

And I feel like a traitor for being relieved.

I have spent fourteen years thinking of nights as a kind of tribe. There is a way of talking about them — the black humour, the exaggerations, the stories about the one that got away, the pride of it — and I have been part of that for over a decade, and I am walking off the end of it, and part of me feels as though I have left something behind that I am not going to be able to explain to anybody who was not there.

I have written enough complaints about the NHS to last several lifetimes and I am not going to write another one here. This is not about staffing. It is not about the rota or the money or the pressure. It is about something much smaller and much harder to fix, which is that for fourteen years I was part of a small group of people who did a difficult thing well, and now I am not.

---

So. Monday.

I do not know what I will be like on days. I have a whole new set of hours to learn and a whole new version of the department to get used to, and I expect to be mediocre at it for a while.

But here is what I know. Some time around four o'clock on Monday morning, somebody will walk into the staff room and put four slices in the toaster, and nobody will admit to starting it. It has never once been admitted to. Nobody knows. It goes on.

And Folasade will be up there on the seventh floor, doing the thing she has done for twenty-two years, and she will still beat me up those stairs, and I intend to be the one who brings her a cup of tea.

I am not sure yet what my version of this will be. But I am going to find out. There will be toast at 4am. I know that much.

---

A few notes on choices, so you can change them if you disagree:

- **The old gentleman** is deliberately thin — no ward, no diagnosis, no dates, no physical detail beyond what you'd already said. If you want it even safer, cut the "went home three days later" line and leave just the hands.
- **The complaint material** is mostly cut, as you asked. The only slightly pointed line is about daytime kindness costing less than night kindness — that's a comment about the department's culture, not staffing, but you may want to soften it if your colleagues are the audience.
- **The ending** lands on the toast and Folasade rather than on you, as you wanted. If you'd rather it end on your sister, that would also work and might be the better last line, honestly.
- **"Hull"** — I made up the resus shout. If that's not your department's word, change it. If you'd rather not have a patient in it at all, Folasade shouting at a crashing set of observations would do the same job without anyone in the bay.

Say the word and I'll do a shorter version for the blog itself with the Thursday-when-it-lands framing, or a version cut to about 900 words if that's closer to what you'd actually post.
